newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Mladic, Bosnian Serb leader seek compromise.
newsitem.headline: Mladic, Bosnian Serb leader seek compromise.

text.p: General Ratko Mladic, defying dismissal as commander of the Bosnian Serb Army with the support of his senior generals, met President Biljana Plavsic on Wednesday to discuss a compromise, military sources said.

Plavsic talked to Mladic at his east Bosnian headquarters in Han Piesak where he has led a fight against attempts by civilians authorities to replace the army's wartime command with junior officers hastily promoted to general rank.
The standoff between the top general and the government thrust into the open divisions in the civilian leadership which is embarrassed by its failure to persuade Mladic to disappear.

The sources said Plavsic regretted having been pushed into the attempt to dislodge Mladic by former President Radovan Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik, the Bosnian Serb member of Bosnia's inter-ethnic presidency.
Karadzic is supposed to have no public role in Bosnian politics after having been driven from office earlier this year because of U.N. indictments for war crimes.
Mladic has also been indicted and both men are resisting extradition to the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.

But Karadzic appears to have maintained his influence with the Bosnian Serb hardliners led by Krajisnik who are determined to retard the Bosnian peace agreement while trying to shape it in their favour.
Bosnian Serb sources said Karadzic and Krajisnik met several times before the general staff purge was announced 10 days ago in an apparent bid to weaken the army as a threat to civilian authority.
The hardliners have built up the Bosnian Serb police as the basis of their power, as Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic did when he pulled Yugoslav troops out of Croatia and Bosnia in 1992.
Karadzic also wants revenge for his humiliation last year when he failed in a similar attempt to dismiss Mladic and other generals who criticised the corruption of the civilian leadership.
Military sources said members of the old general staff who negotiated with Plavsic agreed that Mladic, with war crimes charges hanging over him, cannot remain as the army's post-war commander.
But they believed he should be treated honourably and that the new generals are not up to the job of reorganising and commanding the army.
The new commander, General Pero Colic, and his immediate deputies command little support among senior officers.
Although they dismiss Mladic and his aides as "armchair generals", they are alleged not to have completed the advanced military studies that go with leadership at the highest level.
The sources said Plavsic, who inherited her military advisers from Karadzic, had similar reservations about the capacities of Colic who is a Karadzic and Krajisnik protege.
Her dilemma was to backtrack on the general staff sackings and appointments without losing credibility, they added.
One solution under consideration during the crisis would be to get rid of Colic and replace him with a general who can command the respect of Mladic and the officers loyal to him.
Signs of a compromise emerged this week when police combat readiness in eastern Bosnia was lowered and telephone lines to Mladic's Han Piesak bunker restored.
Military sources said police and troops in Han Piesak agreed early in the dispute that they would not fight.

The attempt to sack Mladic revived the struggle for power between Pale, the hardliners' wartime stronghold outside Sarajevo, and the northern industrial city of Banja Luka which is the new government seat.
Although Plavsic is herself a known hardliner, political sources said she was increasingly irritated by the remnants of Pale's influence and control over Bosnian Serb television.
A source close to her office said she planned to consolidate th government in Banja Luka and transfer the television centre there from Pale.
"It is almost unbelievable that the first news item on television is always Krajisnik and not the president," the source added. "This is inadmissible."
